turns.text:
# ISO 27001 Gap Analysis and 6-Month Roadmap

## Context assumptions

- 250 staff, financial services (so expect regulatory overlap: GLBA, SOX, PCI DSS, or local equivalents depending on jurisdiction)
- Hybrid: Azure + SaaS, with sensitive data on-prem
- Informal ITIL-style change and incident processes
- No ISMS, no risk register
- Target: certification in 12–18 months

Given the sector, auditors and regulators will scrutinize access control, cryptography, logging, supplier risk, and business continuity especially closely.

## Prioritized gap-analysis checklist

I've grouped gaps into three tiers based on what typically blocks certification and what regulators in financial services care about most. Each row shows the ISO 27001:2022 reference, the likely current state for your profile, evidence to collect, and a quick remediation step.

### Tier 1 — Foundational (must exist before Stage 1 audit)

| Area | ISO reference | Likely gap | Evidence to collect | Quick remediation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISMS scope and context | Clause 4 | No documented scope | Scope statement, context analysis, interested parties register | Draft a 2–3 page scope document covering legal entities, locations, cloud tenants, and data types |
| Leadership and policy | Clause 5, A.5.1 | No formal ISMS policy signed by top management | Signed information security policy, roles and responsibilities matrix | Appoint an ISMS owner (often CISO or head of IT), draft top-level policy, get board sign-off |
| Risk management | Clause 6.1, A.5 | No risk register, no methodology | Risk methodology, risk register, risk treatment plan, Statement of Applicability | Adopt a simple methodology (likelihood × impact, 5x5), run an initial workshop, log top 20–30 risks |
| Statement of Applicability | Clause 6.1.3 | Does not exist | SoA covering all 93 Annex A controls with justification | Build from a template; mark each control as applicable or not and reference the relevant policy |
| Asset inventory | A.5.9 | Partial, likely scattered across spreadsheets and Azure | Asset register covering information, hardware, software, cloud services, suppliers | Consolidate Azure Resource Graph, SaaS inventory (via SSO logs), and on-prem CMDB into one register |
| Access control policy | A.5.15, 5.16, 5.18, 8.2 | Informal, likely inconsistent across SaaS apps | Access control policy, joiner-mover-leaver (JML) process, access review records, privileged account list | Document JML, enforce SSO where possible, run a first quarterly access review |

### Tier 2 — Core controls (build during months 2–5)

| Area | ISO reference | Likely gap | Evidence to collect | Quick remediation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Supplier and cloud risk | A.5.19–5.23 | Likely no formal supplier security assessments | Supplier register, security questionnaires, contract clauses, cloud shared responsibility matrix | Classify suppliers by criticality; start with top 10 (Azure, core SaaS, data processors) |
| Cryptography | A.8.24 | Likely inconsistent key management | Cryptography policy, key inventory, encryption standards for data at rest and in transit | Document Azure Key Vault usage, define approved algorithms, address on-prem encryption gaps |
| Logging and monitoring | A.8.15, 8.16 | Logs exist but likely not centralized or reviewed | Logging standard, SIEM or Log Analytics config, alert runbooks, review records | Enable Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Sentinel (or equivalent), define log retention (financial services often requires 1–7 years) |
| Change management | A.8.32 | Informal ITIL process | Change policy, CAB minutes, change records, emergency change procedure | Formalize your existing ITIL-ish process: ticket template, approval matrix, post-implementation review |
| Incident management | A.5.24–5.28 | Informal | Incident response plan, playbooks, incident log, lessons learned | Document IR plan with roles, severity levels, and escalation paths; run a tabletop exercise |
| Backup | A.8.13 | Likely exists but untested | Backup policy, backup inventory, restore test records | Document what is backed up and where; schedule a quarterly restore test |
| Business continuity and DR | A.5.29, 5.30 | Likely no formal BCP or DR plan | BIA, BCP, DR plan, test records | Run a BIA for top 5 critical services, draft a BCP, schedule a DR test |
| Vulnerability management | A.8.8 | Ad hoc patching | Vulnerability management policy, scan reports, patching SLAs, remediation evidence | Enable Defender for Cloud vulnerability assessment; define SLAs (e.g. critical in 7 days, high in 30) |
| Secure configuration | A.8.9 | Baseline likely undocumented | Hardening standards, Azure Policy, CIS benchmarks | Adopt CIS Azure Foundations Benchmark; enable Azure Policy for baseline enforcement |

### Tier 3 — Supporting controls (months 4–6)

| Area | ISO reference | Likely gap | Evidence to collect | Quick remediation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HR security | A.6.1–6.6 | Partial | Background check records, confidentiality agreements, disciplinary process, training records | Align with HR; document screening for roles with access to sensitive data |
| Awareness training | A.6.3 | Likely ad hoc | Training plan, completion records, phishing test results | Roll out a platform (KnowBe4, Hoxhunt, Microsoft Attack Simulator) with quarterly campaigns |
| Physical security | A.7.1–7.14 | On-prem sites need documentation | Site access logs, visitor logs, equipment disposal records | Document controls for on-prem rooms holding sensitive data; include secure disposal |
| Data classification | A.5.12, 5.13 | Likely informal | Classification scheme, labeling guidance, handling rules | Define 3–4 tiers (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted); pilot Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels |
| Secure development | A.8.25–8.28 | Depends on in-house development | SDLC policy, code review records, SAST/DAST reports | If you have devs, document SDLC; if purely SaaS consumers, mark as not applicable in SoA |
| Internal audit | Clause 9.2 | Does not exist | Audit programme, audit reports, corrective actions | Schedule first internal audit around month 9–10 |
| Management review | Clause 9.3 | Does not exist | Management review minutes, KPIs, decisions | Hold quarterly reviews with the ISMS owner and leadership |

## 6-month roadmap

### Month 1 — Foundation
- Appoint ISMS owner and steering committee
- Draft ISMS scope, context, and interested parties
- Draft top-level information security policy and get board approval
- Choose risk methodology
- Select tooling: GRC platform (Vanta, Drata, Tugboat Logic, or a well-maintained spreadsheet for budget reasons) and SIEM approach
- Decide on the certification body for a readiness assessment later

### Month 2 — Risk and assets
- Build consolidated asset inventory
- Run risk workshops with department heads; populate the risk register
- Draft the Statement of Applicability
- Begin supplier register and classify top suppliers
- Document access control policy and JML process

### Month 3 — Core policies and controls
- Draft remaining policies: access control, cryptography, logging, change, incident, backup, acceptable use, data classification
- Formalize change management on top of your existing ITIL-ish flow
- Centralize logging (Sentinel or equivalent)
- Launch awareness training programme

### Month 4 — Operations and testing
- Document incident response plan and run a tabletop
- Document BCP and DR; run a BIA
- Start vulnerability scanning and define remediation SLAs
- Implement secure configuration baselines (CIS)
- Run first quarterly access review

### Month 5 — Supplier, HR, and physical
- Complete security questionnaires for top 10 suppliers
- Review and update contracts with data processing and security clauses
- Formalize HR security controls with HR team
- Document physical security for on-prem sites
- Run a backup restore test

### Month 6 — Readiness
- Complete evidence collection for all applicable Annex A controls
- Run an internal gap assessment (consider an external consultant)
- Address top findings
- Schedule Stage 1 audit for month 9–10, Stage 2 for month 12–15
- Hold first management review

## Practical tips for your profile

Financial services auditors will push hard on **segregation of duties**, **privileged access**, and **evidence of continuous monitoring**. Build these into the design rather than retrofitting.

Your hybrid model means the **cloud shared responsibility matrix** should be explicit in your SoA. Azure handles a lot, but your configuration, identity, and data classification remain yours.

GRC tooling (Vanta, Drata, Secureframe) can compress the evidence-collection timeline significantly for Azure and SaaS-heavy environments. For 250 staff, the cost is usually justified by the time saved.

Don't over-engineer policies. Auditors want to see that what you've written matches what you actually do. A short, honest policy you follow beats a long aspirational one you don't.

Want me to go deeper on any specific area — for example, drafting the risk methodology, building a Statement of Applicability template, or sketching out the supplier assessment process?

## Part 2 — Risk Methodology

### Document control header

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Document title | Information Security Risk Management Methodology |
| Document ID | ISMS-DOC-002 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Owner | CISO |
| Approved by | [Name, Title] |
| Approval date | [Date] |
| Next review | Annually |

### 1. Purpose

This methodology defines how [Organization Name] identifies, analyzes, evaluates, treats, and monitors information security risks in accordance with ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Clause 6.1 and ISO/IEC 27005 guidance.

### 2. Scope

Applies to all risks affecting the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of information assets within the ISMS scope.

### 3. Risk management process

The process follows a continuous cycle: Establish context → Identify → Analyze → Evaluate → Treat → Monitor and review → Communicate and consult.

### 4. Risk identification

Risks are identified through:
- Asset-based analysis (per asset in the register, consider threats and vulnerabilities)
- Threat intelligence feeds and sector-specific sources (e.g. FS-ISAC)
- Incident post-mortems
- Internal and external audits
- Vulnerability scans
- Workshops with business units (minimum annual)
- Supplier assessments

Each identified risk is recorded in the Risk Register with a unique ID, description, affected assets, threat, vulnerability, and owner.

### 5. Risk analysis — 5×5 matrix

#### 5.1 Likelihood scale

| Score | Rating | Definition | Frequency guidance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rare | May occur only in exceptional circumstances | Less than once every 5 years |
| 2 | Unlikely | Could occur at some time | Once every 2–5 years |
| 3 | Possible | Might occur at some point | Once every 1–2 years |
| 4 | Likely | Will probably occur in most circumstances | Multiple times per year |
| 5 | Almost certain | Expected to occur frequently | Monthly or more often |

Likelihood is assessed considering threat capability, threat motivation, vulnerability exposure, and existing controls.

#### 5.2 Impact scale

Impact is assessed across four dimensions. The highest applicable score sets the impact rating.

| Score | Rating | Financial | Operational | Regulatory / Legal | Reputational |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Negligible | <$10k | Minor disruption, <1 hour | Minor policy breach, no external reporting | Internal only |
| 2 | Minor | $10k–$100k | Single service degraded, <1 day | Reportable to internal audit | Minor customer complaints |
| 3 | Moderate | $100k–$500k | Multiple services disrupted, 1–3 days | Regulatory notification required | Local media coverage |
| 4 | Major | $500k–$2M | Core service outage, 3–7 days | Regulatory fine or sanction likely | National media, significant customer loss |
| 5 | Severe | >$2M | Prolonged outage, >7 days, inability to operate | Loss of license, criminal liability, significant fines | Sustained reputational damage, existential threat |

Financial services organizations should calibrate the financial scale against their risk appetite and regulatory capital requirements.

#### 5.3 Inherent risk score

**Inherent Risk Score = Likelihood × Impact** (range: 1 to 25)

This is the risk level before considering existing controls.

For readability I've laid out each risk in a block rather than a single wide table. The field order matches the CSV schema above.

### RISK-2026-001 — Privileged access abuse

- **Description:** Malicious or negligent misuse of privileged accounts in Azure and on-prem systems leading to unauthorized changes, data exfiltration, or service disruption.
- **Affected asset / owner:** Azure AD privileged roles; on-prem domain admin accounts / CISO
- **Threat / vulnerability:** Malicious insider or compromised admin credential / Standing privileged access without JIT; limited monitoring
- **CIA:** C, I, A
- **Inherent L×I:** 4 × 5 = 20 (Critical)
- **Current controls:** MFA on admin accounts; named accounts only; quarterly review
- **Control effectiveness:** Partially Effective
- **Residual L×I:** 3 × 4 = 12 (High)
- **Treatment:** Mitigate — Implement Azure PIM with JIT for Tier 0/1 roles; PAM solution for on-prem; dedicated monitoring in Sentinel
- **Target residual:** 6 (Medium)
- **Owner / target date:** CISO / 2026-09-30
- **Annex A:** A.5.15; A.5.18; A.8.2; A.8.15; A.8.16

### RISK-2026-002 — Ransomware attack

- **Description:** Ransomware encrypts production systems and backups, causing extended outage and potential data loss across cloud and on-prem environments.
- **Affected asset / owner:** Production servers (cloud and on-prem); file shares; backup repositories / IT Operations Manager
- **Threat / vulnerability:** Organized cybercrime group / Delayed patching; backup repositories reachable from production network
- **CIA:** I, A
- **Inherent L×I:** 4 × 5 = 20 (Critical)
- **Current controls:** EDR; email filtering; backups; awareness training
- **Control effectiveness:** Partially Effective
- **Residual L×I:** 3 × 4 = 12 (High)
- **Treatment:** Mitigate — Immutable backups; segregated backup vault; accelerated patching SLAs; IR tabletop; MDR service
- **Target residual:** 6 (Medium)
- **Owner / target date:** CISO / 2026-10-31
- **Annex A:** A.8.7; A.8.8; A.8.13; A.5.24; A.5.26; A.5.30

### RISK-2026-003 — Cloud misconfiguration

- **Description:** Misconfigured Azure resources (public storage, overly permissive NSGs, exposed management ports, weak IAM) leading to data exposure or unauthorized access.
- **Affected asset / owner:** Azure subscriptions and resources / Cloud Platform Lead
- **Threat / vulnerability:** External attacker scanning for exposed assets / No formal baseline; limited guardrails; manual deployments
- **CIA:** C, I
- **Inherent L×I:** 4 × 4 = 16 (Critical)
- **Current controls:** Defender for Cloud (basic); some Azure Policy assignments
- **Control effectiveness:** Partially Effective
- **Residual L×I:** 3 × 4 = 12 (High)
- **Treatment:** Mitigate — Adopt CIS Azure Foundations Benchmark; enforce via Azure Policy; enable Defender for Cloud standard tier; move to IaC with pipeline scanning
- **Target residual:** 4 (Low)
- **Owner / target date:** Cloud Platform Lead / 2026-09-30
- **Annex A:** A.8.9; A.8.22; A.8.23; A.8.32

### RISK-2026-004 — Third-party data breach

- **Description:** Breach at a critical supplier (SaaS provider or data processor) exposes customer or employee personal and financial data, triggering regulatory and contractual obligations.
- **Affected asset / owner:** Customer data held by Tier 1 suppliers / Data Protection Officer
- **Threat / vulnerability:** Supplier compromise / No formal supplier security assessment programme; contracts lack security clauses for some suppliers
- **CIA:** C
- **Inherent L×I:** 3 × 5 = 15 (High)
- **Current controls:** Some supplier SOC 2 reports reviewed ad hoc; NDAs in place
- **Control effectiveness:** Ineffective
- **Residual L×I:** 3 × 5 = 15 (High)
- **Treatment:** Mitigate + Transfer — Complete supplier register with tiering; security questionnaires for Tier 1; contract clauses for breach notification and audit rights; cyber insurance review
- **Target residual:** 6 (Medium)
- **Owner / target date:** Procurement Lead with CISO / 2026-11-30
- **Annex A:** A.5.19; A.5.20; A.5.21; A.5.22; A.5.23

### RISK-2026-005 — Backup failure or unrecoverable backup

- **Description:** Backups fail silently, are incomplete, or cannot be restored when needed, leading to permanent data loss during incident recovery.
- **Affected asset / owner:** Backup systems; backed-up data / IT Operations Manager
- **Threat / vulnerability:** Technical failure; ransomware targeting backups / No regular restore testing; no documented RTO/RPO per service

## Part 1 — Remaining entries (readable format)

### RISK-2026-005 — Backup failure or unrecoverable backup

- **Description:** Backups fail silently, are incomplete, or cannot be restored when needed, leading to permanent data loss during incident recovery.
- **Affected asset / owner:** Backup systems; backed-up data / IT Operations Manager
- **Threat / vulnerability:** Technical failure; ransomware targeting backups / No regular restore testing; no documented RTO/RPO per service; limited backup monitoring
- **CIA:** I, A
- **Inherent L×I:** 3 × 5 = 15 (High)
- **Current controls:** Daily backups configured; Azure Backup for cloud workloads; Veeam for on-prem
- **Control effectiveness:** Partially Effective
- **Residual L×I:** 3 × 4 = 12 (High)
- **Treatment:** Mitigate — Implement quarterly restore testing; define and document RTO/RPO per service; configure backup failure alerting; implement immutable backup copies
- **Target residual:** 4 (Low)
- **Owner / target date:** IT Operations Manager / 2026-08-31
- **Annex A:** A.8.13; A.8.14; A.5.30; A.8.16

### RISK-2026-006 — Unapproved SaaS (Shadow IT)

- **Description:** Employees adopt unapproved SaaS applications, storing or processing company data outside IT governance, bypassing security controls and creating data leakage, compliance, and licensing risks.
- **Affected asset / owner:** Company data in unknown SaaS applications / CISO
- **Threat / vulnerability:** Employee convenience-driven adoption; departmental procurement / No CASB or app discovery; permissive expense policy; limited user awareness of SaaS risks
- **CIA:** C, I
- **Inherent L×I:** 4 × 3 = 12 (High)
- **Current controls:** Acceptable Use Policy; expense review by Finance
- **Control effectiveness:** Ineffective
- **Residual L×I:** 4 × 3 = 12 (High)
- **Treatment:** Mitigate — Deploy Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps (CASB) for discovery and control; establish SaaS approval workflow; update AUP and run targeted awareness; quarterly SaaS review with Finance
- **Target residual:** 6 (Medium)
- **Owner / target date:** CISO / 2026-10-31
- **Annex A:** A.5.9; A.5.10; A.5.23; A.8.1; A.6.3

### RISK-2026-007 — Phishing and credential theft

- **Description:** Successful phishing attack results in credential compromise, account takeover, business email compromise, or malware delivery, potentially leading to financial fraud, data breach, or ransomware entry.
- **Affected asset / owner:** User accounts; email system; downstream systems accessible via SSO / CISO
- **Threat / vulnerability:** External threat actors (cybercrime, BEC groups) / Human susceptibility; sophisticated phishing lures; some legacy accounts without MFA
- **CIA:** C, I, A
- **Inherent L×I:** 5 × 4 = 20 (Critical)
- **Current controls:** Microsoft Defender for Office 365; MFA on most accounts; annual awareness training; SPF/DKIM/DMARC configured
- **Control effectiveness:** Partially Effective
- **Residual L×I:** 4 × 3 = 12 (High)
- **Treatment:** Mitigate — Enforce phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2) for privileged and finance users; monthly phishing simulations with targeted follow-up; enable DMARC enforcement (p=reject); enhanced BEC detection rules in Sentinel
- **Target residual:** 6 (Medium)
- **Owner / target date:** CISO / 2026-09-30
- **Annex A:** A.5.17; A.6.3; A.8.5; A.8.23; A.5.24

### RISK-2026-008 — Business continuity failure

- **Description:** Failure to maintain critical business operations during a disruptive event (major outage, cyber incident, physical event affecting on-prem site) due to untested or inadequate continuity arrangements, leading to prolonged service outage, regulatory breach, and customer loss.
- **Affected asset / owner:** Critical business services; on-prem data center; core applications / CISO and Business Continuity Lead
- **Threat / vulnerability:** Major cyber incident; data center failure; regional disruption / No formal BIA; no tested BCP; DR plan for cloud exists but on-prem DR unclear; single-site dependency for sensitive data
- **CIA:** A
- **Inherent L×I:** 3 × 5 = 15 (High)
- **Current controls:** Azure region redundancy for cloud workloads; informal recovery knowledge among IT staff
- **Control effectiveness:** Ineffective
- **Residual L×I:** 3 × 5 = 15 (High)
- **Treatment:** Mitigate — Conduct BIA for top 10 services; develop formal BCP and DR plan; establish secondary site or Azure DR for on-prem sensitive data; annual tabletop and biennial full DR test; define and communicate RTO/RPO
- **Target residual:** 6 (Medium)
- **Owner / target date:** CISO with Business Continuity Lead / 2026-12-31
- **Annex A:** A.5.29; A.5.30; A.8.14; A.8.13
